questions.q: What specific problem does an ADR solve that a verbal decision made 'in a meeting' does not?
options: It creates a durable, written record that doesn't rely on anyone's memory, preventing the decision from being lost, misremembered, or re-litigated from scratch later
ADRs make decisions happen faster than meetings do
ADRs are required by law for all software architecture decisions
There is no real difference -- a meeting and an ADR serve identical purposes
questions.explain: A decision that only lives in people's memory is an oral tradition -- it gets revised, forgotten, and re-argued; a written ADR fixes the decision, its reasoning, and its trade-offs in a durable, shared place.

questions.q: In the standard ADR structure, what does the 'Consequences' section honestly include?
options: Both positive and negative trade-offs that were explicitly accepted by making this decision, not just the benefits
Only the benefits of the chosen option, omitting any downsides
A list of unrelated decisions made by other teams
The personal opinions of whoever wrote the ADR, unrelated to the actual decision
questions.explain: A useful ADR names real downsides honestly (e.g., vendor lock-in, a future cost threshold) alongside the benefits -- an ADR that only lists positives isn't being honest about what was actually accepted.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say the 'Alternatives Considered' section is often MORE valuable than the decision itself?
options: The most common question a Staff/Principal engineer gets asked is 'why didn't we choose the other option' -- having that reasoning already written down avoids reconstructing it from memory later, possibly after the original decision-maker has left
Alternatives Considered is purely a formality with no practical value
The decision section is always less important than any other section of an ADR
Alternatives Considered exists only to make the document longer
questions.explain: Documenting rejected alternatives and why they were rejected answers the question people actually ask most often, and prevents a team from re-evaluating and re-deriving the same rejected conclusion months later.

questions.q: What real, wasteful failure mode does writing down rejected alternatives specifically prevent?
options: A new engineer, unaware a path was already evaluated and rejected, re-proposing it later and the team spending real time re-deriving the same already-reached conclusion
A failure mode where the chosen vector database automatically becomes more expensive over time
A failure mode where ADRs cause software bugs in production
There is no real failure mode this section prevents -- it exists purely for documentation completeness
questions.explain: Without a written record of why an alternative was rejected, that reasoning can be lost -- leading someone to propose the same already-rejected option again and the team wasting time re-evaluating it from scratch.

questions.q: Why does the lesson insist the 'Context' section describe the situation 'as it actually was, not as it looks in hindsight'?
options: A decision that looked reasonable given the information available at the time can look wrong in hindsight after circumstances change -- Context preserves the honest basis for the decision, not a retroactively edited justification
The Context section is purely decorative and has no real purpose
Hindsight always produces a more accurate account of a decision than contemporaneous notes
Context should describe a completely different, unrelated decision for comparison
questions.explain: Capturing the real situation at decision time (not a hindsight-adjusted version) is what lets a future reader fairly judge whether the decision was reasonable given what was actually known then.
